Hakeem Jeffries backs impeaching Pete Hegseth as Dems prepare investigations
Jeffries said Hegseth “has got to go” and described himself as a “hard yes” on a resolution to impeach the secretary.
Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next Speaker of the House if Democrats regain control of the chamber, says he would support impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Hegseth is among several members of the Trump administration whom Democrats are expected to target with investigations when they take control of Congress in January.
During an interview on ABC’s “This Week,” Jeffries said Hegseth “has got to go” and described himself as a “hard yes” on a resolution to impeach the secretary that is expected to come before the House this week.
“The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe,” Jeffries claimed.
Hegseth has been a target of those who are critical of the Trump administration over the ongoing war with Iran. Republican Representative Thomas Massie, who is retiring at the end of his term after losing his primary election, is expected to force a House vote this week on impeaching Hegseth.
Massie previously attempted to bring the resolution forward before the midterm elections, but House Speaker Mike Johnson called an early recess, preventing a vote on the measure. Impeachment resolutions must be taken up within two legislative days of their introduction.
Massie is expected to renew his efforts this week, though Hegseth’s impeachment is unlikely under the current Republican majority. Additionally, a successful impeachment would not automatically remove Hegseth from office. Removal would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate.
Attorney General Todd Blanche told CNN on Sunday that the Justice Department would defend members of the Trump administration against impeachment efforts and investigations. He said he would be “very worried” if he were a Democrat threatening to investigate administration officials.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Aprnell also stated that Hegseth “will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists.”
“The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America,” the statement added, per The Washington Post.

‘I’m a hard yes’: Hakeem Jeffries announces support for Hegseth impeachment
sources.text:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) came out in support of impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Sunday, telling ABC News he’s a “hard yes.”
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “Pete Hegseth has got to go.”
Asked by “This Week” co-anchor Jonathan Karl if he’s confident all House Democrats will join him in supporting the potential resolution, Jeffries said his conference will “have that conversation” on Tuesday morning, when members convene in Washington for the first time since the midterm election.
“But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution,” Jeffries said.
Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican lawmaker who has often clashed with President Donald Trump, told ABC News he intends to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday. By raising a question of privilege on the floor, leaders are required to schedule a vote on it within two legislative days.
Massie’s resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing the defense secretary of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, in addition to other alleged offenses.
Thus far, Trump has defended Hegseth, telling reporters Thursday that he has “done a fantastic job.” The president also told Karl the same day, “I have every intention to keep him.”
Hegseth also defended himself Thursday in a video posted on social media.
“A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction – didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me.”
‘Irresponsible’ decision to make Stephen Miller chief of staff
Jeffries, who is likely to become the next speaker of the House in January, said Sunday that he has still not spoken to Trump since the midterm elections, which he described as a “tremendous repudiation of MAGA extremism.”
“The country clearly has had enough. And we got to fight for an affordable America,” Jeffries said. “People are drowning in this failed Republican economy. And enough is enough in that regard. That’s why we’re going to fight to lower the high cost of living on all the things. And we have to.”
While Trump told ABC News in a phone interview after the election that he thinks he can work with Democrats, Jeffries questioned the president’s intentions, given his decision announced Friday to elevate White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump loyalist, to the position of White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
“It’s an awful choice. Stephen Miller is the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine and has unleashed billions of taxpayer dollars to brutalize and kill American citizens, like Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, and at the same period of time to violently target law-abiding, immigrant families and communities all across the country. So, you know, it was an irresponsible decision in my view,” Jeffries said.
“There’s not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we’re committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people,” he added.
Karl pressed Jeffries to clarify if he means that he won’t be able to communicate with Miller in the way he sometimes communicated with outgoing chief of staff Wiles.
“It’s not going to happen with the new chief of staff to the extent that he lacks — because he clearly represents, along with Pete Hegseth and a few others, a really toxic brand of political engagement, of politics and of governance. And the American people just voted for that kind of MAGA extremism to be eradicated,” Jeffries said.
Democratic priorities for legislation and investigations
Bringing down costs for housing, groceries, gas and healthcare will be top priorities for his party in the new Congress, Jeffries said, as well as ending the war with Iran, stopping “the Trump tariffs,” and “[reversing] the Medicaid cuts that put the health insurance of millions of Americans at risk and threatens to close hospitals all over the place.”
“The American people clearly want change that’s bold, change that’s transformational, and change that is dramatic,” Jeffries, said, adding “we certainly need to reverse the SNAP cuts, and we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. And hopefully we’ll see some courage by a few of our colleagues on the other side of the aisle to work on these issues to get things done.”
The Democratic Party is “committed to moving aggressively during the first 100 days of the new Congress and beyond to keep our word,” said Jeffries.
According to ABC News national voter polls, 55% of voters who voted for U.S. House races said that government corruption was “crucial” to their vote; another 36% said it was a “major factor.”
In a two-word statement released late Tuesday after Democrats were projected to take control of the House, Rep. Robert Garcia, the presumptive chairman of the House Oversight Committee, stated: “Lawyer up.”
“Well, there’s a cost to corruption. And throughout this campaign we’ve promised that we would focus certainly on affordability and driving down the high cost of living, and on accountability in the face of the unprecedented corruption that we’ve seen unleashed on the American people by the Trump cartel,” Jeffries said. “We’re committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it’s found. That’s in Congress, in the Supreme Court and with respect to this administration.”
For its part, the administration is saying it will investigate Democrats. Trump said Saturday that he ordered the Department of Justice to examine what he deemed “criminal” acts by Democrats, though he did not provide examples to support his allegations. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday echoed the president’s statement.
“What we’ve seen over the past several days and even over the past several weeks are outright threats, many, many by elected members of Congress and some senators against anybody that’s conservative and anybody that that happens to be a Republican,” Blanche told CNN. “Over the last several days, we’ve seen it, that rhetoric even rise up to the point where they’re already — before they’re even in power, they’re already talking about investigations and impeachments with no basis, no facts, just out there running around — that that should be something that that President Trump is very concerned about. And certainly I am as well.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has declared that US War Secretary Pete Hegseth “has got to go,” saying the Pentagon chief abused power and engineered a costly war of aggression against the Islamic Republic of Iran that has inflicted economic pain on the American people and failed to advance any legitimate security interest.
In an interview with ABC News on Sunday, Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House after Democrats’ midterm gains, said he is a “hard yes” on a forthcoming impeachment resolution against Hegseth.
“The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices for the American people and made the country less safe,” Jeffries stated. “Pete Hegseth has got to go.”
The Democratic leader added that his party intends to prioritize ending the US-Israeli war on Iran once it assumes greater control of Congress.
“We want to do things like end this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has made life way too expensive,” he said. Jeffries predicted “incredibly strong support” among House Democrats for the measure when lawmakers return to Washington this week.
The push has drawn bipartisan criticism. Outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky plans to reintroduce an impeachment resolution as early as Monday, containing multiple articles that accuse Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution by participating in unauthorized hostilities against Iran.
Earlier Democratic-led articles of impeachment, introduced by lawmakers including Representatives Yassamin Ansari and Brittany Pettersen, charged Hegseth with directing unlawful strikes, endangering US troops, and contributing to civilian casualties in Iran, including reported attacks on civilian infrastructure.
Democratic Senator Jack Reed has separately described Hegseth as “unqualified” both operationally and temperamentally, stating that he has turned the Pentagon into a political operation and that it is time for him to resign.
Representative Jake Auchincloss has called Hegseth “unqualified and incompetent” from day one and said impeachment proceedings should be pursued if investigations warrant it.
Ranking Armed Services Committee Democrat Adam Smith has indicated openness to impeaching both Trump and Hegseth over the handling of the war.
Newly elected Democratic Representative Nancy Lacore, a retired Navy vice admiral whom Hegseth dismissed last year during a purge of senior officers, has made ending the war her top priority.
Speaking to CBS’s Face the Nation, Lacore said the war “has driven up costs extraordinarily high across the district and the country.”
She described Hegseth as “the most unqualified secretary that this nation has seen,” adding that he “has caused significant damage to us as a country, put us at risk and damaged the readiness of our entire military force.”
When asked about potential impeachable offenses, Lacore replied that the war itself is “extremely damaging to our country” and can be tied to broader failures of strategy and readiness under Hegseth’s leadership. She noted she was never given a reason for her own removal.
The mounting domestic backlash comes as the US-Israeli war against Iran has failed to achieve its stated objectives while imposing rising fuel and consumer prices on Americans and exposing US forces to prolonged risk.
Critics across the political spectrum now portray the war as a strategic miscalculation driven by political considerations rather than national interest, with Hegseth emerging as a central figure in accountability demands.

sources.text:
House Democrat Leader Hakeem Jeffries endorsed an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the Iran war, as Republican Rep. Thomas Massie prepares to force a congressional vote.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., announced Sunday, Nov. 8, that he supports impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the Pentagon chief of abusing his authority and undermining national security through the Trump administration’s military campaign against Iran.
During an appearance on ABC’s “This Week”, Jeffries endorsed an impeachment resolution being advanced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who plans to introduce the measure as early as Monday.
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe,” Jeffries told co-anchor Jonathan Karl. “Pete Hegseth has got to go.”
The endorsement places the House Democratic leader behind an impeachment initiative originating with a Republican lawmaker who has repeatedly clashed with President Donald Trump over military operations and executive authority.
Massie has indicated that he intends to reintroduce an eight-article impeachment resolution against Hegseth, including allegations involving the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which establishes congressional procedures governing presidential military action.
The Kentucky congressman plans to introduce the measure as a privileged resolution, a parliamentary procedure that would require House leadership to schedule a vote within two legislative days.
Asked whether all House Democrats would support the resolution, Jeffries stopped short of guaranteeing unanimous backing but predicted substantial agreement within his party.
“We’ll certainly have that conversation on Tuesday morning when we reconvene for the first time in Washington, D.C. But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution,” Jeffries said.
The planned discussion comes after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, setting up a shift in congressional leadership when the new Congress convenes in January.
Although Democrats will not formally assume their new majorities until then, Massie’s procedural strategy could bring the impeachment proposal before the current Republican-controlled House.
Hegseth has rejected the impeachment effort, describing the allegations as politically motivated attacks intended to undermine the administration.
In a video posted Thursday, the defense secretary criticized Massie and Democratic lawmakers for pursuing the resolution.
“A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said.
“It’s all about the politics of personal destruction — didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me,” he added.
Trump has also publicly defended Hegseth despite growing criticism of the administration’s military operations.
Speaking to reporters Thursday, the president said Hegseth had “done a fantastic job” and told Karl that he had “every intention to keep him.”
The impeachment dispute centers primarily on the administration’s military campaign against Iran, which critics argue has imposed significant financial costs, contributed to higher consumer prices and raised constitutional questions about congressional authorization for military action.
Massie’s proposed articles include allegations that Hegseth violated the War Powers Resolution, although the legal and constitutional questions surrounding the campaign remain contested.
Jeffries has linked the Iran conflict to broader criticism of the administration’s economic and national security policies, arguing that military spending and rising prices have placed additional burdens on American households.
Hegseth and the White House maintain that the military campaign serves U.S. national security interests and have defended the Pentagon’s conduct.
The impeachment initiative comes as Democrats prepare a broader oversight agenda targeting decisions made during Trump’s second term.
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee when Democrats assume control, has signaled plans for investigations involving administration officials and White House operations.
During Sunday’s interview, Karl asked Jeffries about Garcia’s warning that administration personnel should “lawyer up” in anticipation of congressional scrutiny.
Jeffries defended the prospect of investigations, arguing that Democrats had campaigned on addressing government accountability alongside household affordability.
“There’s a cost to corruption,” Jeffries said, accusing the administration of misconduct and arguing that congressional oversight would be necessary.
Democrats are also considering investigations into Hegseth’s management of the Pentagon, including the removal of senior military officers, decisions involving Ukraine and American military strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels in Latin American waters.
The allegations remain matters of political and legal dispute, and impeachment proceedings would not themselves establish that Hegseth committed wrongdoing.
Under the Constitution, the House of Representatives has the authority to impeach federal civil officers by a simple majority vote. Conviction and removal from office require a two-thirds majority in the Senate.
Because Republicans retain control of Congress through the end of the current session, any immediate impeachment vote would occur before Democrats assume their newly won majorities.
Even if the House approved articles of impeachment, removal would require a separate Senate trial and sufficient votes for conviction.
The Washington Post reported Sunday that Jeffries’ endorsement represents a significant expansion of Democratic support for Massie’s effort, which had previously been associated primarily with the Kentucky Republican’s opposition to the administration’s Iran policy.
The resolution could become an early test of how Democratic lawmakers intend to pursue accountability measures against Trump administration officials following their electoral victories.
For now, Hegseth remains in office with the president’s support, while Jeffries and other Democrats prepare to discuss whether to unite behind Massie’s proposal.
The next development could come Monday, Nov. 9, when Massie is expected to introduce the impeachment resolution, potentially setting up a House vote later in the week.

WASHINGTON — Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader poised to become the next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, joining the growing calls to remove one of President Donald Trump’s top cabinet secretaries after overwhelming Republican defeats in last week’s elections.
Jeffries said that he was a “hard yes” on a resolution to impeach Hegseth that was expected to come to the House floor this week — the first time the top Democrat has publicly expressed support for the idea.
“The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries said during an interview on the ABC morning program This Week, adding, “Pete Hegseth has got to go.”
Democrats, emboldened by decisive victories in the House and the Senate last week, have begun laying the groundwork for an aggressive oversight agenda aimed at Trump and his administration. But increased bipartisan pressure, especially on Hegseth, since the election suggests that a political reckoning could come before the new Congress begins.

Massie first moved to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterms. That prompted Speaker Mike Johnson to call an early recess to avoid voting on the measure. Impeachment resolutions are privileged motions in the House and when introduced must be taken up within two days.
Because that effort expired, Massie must renew his notice to force action on the measure, which he is expected to do when the House returns this week, again setting off a two-day clock to take up the resolution.

Thomas Massie Vows to Force Pete Hegseth Impeachment Vote Within Days as Trump Faces Possible GOP Revolt
House Rule IX requires the Speaker to schedule consideration of a qualifying resolution within two legislative days after a member announces their intention to offer it
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie plans to press for consideration of his impeachment resolution against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth during the week of 9 November, using a procedure that could bring the measure before a chamber controlled by his party.
Massie, a seven-term Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump, set out eight articles of impeachment in a draft resolution in September. Democrats won control of both chambers in the 3 November midterm elections, but Republicans retain control of the outgoing chamber until the new Congress convenes in January.
Rule IX Could Put the Articles on the House Schedule
Massie plans to give fresh notice under House Rule IX when lawmakers return. He read the draft articles on the House floor in September. The House adjourned a day earlier than scheduled, preventing Massie from advancing the resolution before the pre-election recess.
Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, denied that the early adjournment was intended to avoid a vote on the impeachment measure. The resolution was not considered.
The parliamentarian is expected to assess whether the resolution qualifies as a question of privilege, but the Speaker makes the formal ruling when it is called up. If the resolution qualifies, Rule IX requires the Speaker to designate a time for its consideration within two legislative days after Massie announces to the House his intention to offer it and its form. That does not guarantee a direct vote on the impeachment charges.
Republicans could instead move to table the resolution, disposing of it without deciding whether to impeach Hegseth.
Massie Predicts Support, but No Vote Count Is Public
Massie told Roll Call on 26 October that he gave the resolution a better than a 50% chance of passing. He expected Democrats to support it and said some Republicans might be more willing to back impeachment after their campaigns had ended.
Axios reported on 8 November that Republican leaders were bracing for enough defections to impeach Hegseth. That remains a possibility, not a confirmed tally. Attendance could also affect the result in a closely divided House.
Iran Allegations Lead the Eight Articles
The articles accuse Hegseth of abusing his authority in overseeing US military operations, particularly the war in Iran. They allege violations of the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which requires consultation with Congress and a report within 48 hours in specified circumstances. It generally requires US forces to be withdrawn within 60 days after the report is submitted or due, whichever comes first.
The president may extend the period by up to 30 days if he certifies in writing that unavoidable military necessity requires continued use of the forces to ensure their safe withdrawal.
The other articles allege unlawful operations involving Venezuela, including the capture of Nicolás Maduro, military action in Yemen and strikes against suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. They also accuse Hegseth of disregarding civilian protections and retaliating against Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat, over his criticism of the administration. These are allegations in Massie's resolution, not established findings.
Hegseth called the articles a sham. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told Axios the Department of War had followed the law.
House Impeachment Would Not Ensure Removal
A simple majority in the House could impeach Hegseth, but conviction and removal in the Senate would require a two-thirds vote of senators present. In 2024, senators dismissed impeachment charges against Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas as unconstitutional without holding a trial.
William Belknap, the first Cabinet secretary impeached, resigned as secretary of war in 1876 shortly before the House voted to impeach him. The Senate nevertheless held a trial and acquitted him. Massie has indicated he intends to pursue the vote only if Hegseth remains in the job. He plans to press ahead during the lame-duck session.

Massie's Articles Target War Powers, Military Action
Massie’s 34-page resolution, which he originally read on the House floor in September, outlines eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth.
Article I alleges that Hegseth, in his capacity as defense secretary, executed unlawful orders in contravention of Section 2(c) of the War Powers Resolution of 1973. The resolution argues that Congress has the constitutional authority to initiate war and alleges that the administration introduced U.S. forces into hostilities without a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization or a national emergency created by an attack on the United States.

He also dismissed speculation that Hegseth could be moved into another role, saying he had not heard discussions about appointing him to a Senate vacancy.

While Jeffries stated his individual position was clear, he did not guarantee the entire Democratic caucus would vote in favor of the resolution.
“We’ll certainly have that conversation on Tuesday morning when we reconvene for the first time in Washington, D.C.,” Jeffries, who could possibly be the next House speaker, said. “But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution.”

Garcia explained the meaning of this post by saying: ‘When Republicans go low, what we’re not gonna do anymore is just take the high road and turn the other cheek.’
Garcia’s outspoken comments since election night have prompted responses from prominent conservatives and Trump administration officials, including former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt and Attorney General Todd Blanche.
After Garcia issued a statement through the Oversight Committee saying, ‘Stephen Miller should lawyer up,’ Blanche responded on X: ‘The Chief of Staff already has a lawyer. The Attorney General of the United States and the Department of Justice.’
Garcia answered: ‘While we have your attention, when are you coming in to testify under oath about covering up the Epstein files? Or are you too scared to come in?’
During an interview with Lara Trump on Fox News on Saturday night, Leavitt said: ‘You had Rep Garcia’s first statement after election night was “Lawyer up.”‘
‘This is a party whose base is hellbent on political retribution, obstructionism, impeachment – they don’t want to do what’s best for the voters who elected them,’ Leavitt said.
Garcia has occasionally adopted a more playful tone. On his personal X account, he shared an image of the clown from the horror film It peering from a sewer, captioned: ‘When they go low this is me.’
Explaining the post on CNN, Garcia said: ‘This is a joke. I mean, basically what I’m saying is when Republicans go low, what we’re not gonna do anymore is just take the high road and turn the other cheek. We’re gonna get down and be in that fight.’

‘I’m a hard yes’: Hakeem Jeffries announces support for Hegseth impeachment
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) came out in support of impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Sunday, telling ABC News he's a "hard yes."
"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe," Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week." "Pete Hegseth has got to go."
Asked by "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl if he's confident all House Democrats will join him in supporting the potential resolution, Jeffries said his conference will "have that conversation" on Tuesday morning, when members convene in Washington for the first time since the midterm election.
"But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution," Jeffries said.
Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican lawmaker who has often clashed with President Donald Trump, told ABC News he intends to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday. By raising a question of privilege on the floor, leaders are required to schedule a vote on it within two legislative days.
Massie’s resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing the defense secretary of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, in addition to other alleged offenses.
Thus far, Trump has defended Hegseth, telling reporters Thursday that he has “done a fantastic job.” The president also told Karl the same day, “I have every intention to keep him.”
Hegseth also defended himself Thursday in a video posted on social media.
“A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said. “It's all about the politics of personal destruction — didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me.”
‘Irresponsible’ decision to make Stephen Miller chief of staff
Jeffries, who is likely to become the next speaker of the House in January, said Sunday that he has still not spoken to Trump since the midterm elections, which he described as a "tremendous repudiation of MAGA extremism."
"The country clearly has had enough. And we got to fight for an affordable America," Jeffries said. "People are drowning in this failed Republican economy. And enough is enough in that regard. That’s why we’re going to fight to lower the high cost of living on all the things. And we have to."
While Trump told ABC News in a phone interview after the election that he thinks he can work with Democrats, Jeffries questioned the president's intentions, given his decision announced Friday to elevate White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump loyalist, to the position of White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
"It’s an awful choice. Stephen Miller is the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine and has unleashed billions of taxpayer dollars to brutalize and kill American citizens, like Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, and at the same period of time to violently target law-abiding, immigrant families and communities all across the country. So, you know, it was an irresponsible decision in my view," Jeffries said.
"There’s not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we’re committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people," he added.
Karl pressed Jeffries to clarify if he means that he won't be able to communicate with Miller in the way he sometimes communicated with outgoing chief of staff Wiles.
"It’s not going to happen with the new chief of staff to the extent that he lacks -- because he clearly represents, along with Pete Hegseth and a few others, a really toxic brand of political engagement, of politics and of governance. And the American people just voted for that kind of MAGA extremism to be eradicated," Jeffries said.
Democratic priorities for legislation and investigations
Bringing down costs for housing, groceries, gas and healthcare will be top priorities for his party in the new Congress, Jeffries said, as well as ending the war with Iran, stopping "the Trump tariffs," and "[reversing] the Medicaid cuts that put the health insurance of millions of Americans at risk and threatens to close hospitals all over the place."
"The American people clearly want change that’s bold, change that’s transformational, and change that is dramatic," Jeffries, said, adding "we certainly need to reverse the SNAP cuts, and we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. And hopefully we’ll see some courage by a few of our colleagues on the other side of the aisle to work on these issues to get things done."
The Democratic Party is "committed to moving aggressively during the first 100 days of the new Congress and beyond to keep our word," said Jeffries.
According to ABC News national voter polls, 55% of voters who voted for U.S. House races said that government corruption was "crucial" to their vote; another 36% said it was a "major factor."
In a two-word statement released late Tuesday after Democrats were projected to take control of the House, Rep. Robert Garcia, the presumptive chairman of the House Oversight Committee, stated: "Lawyer up."
"Well, there’s a cost to corruption. And throughout this campaign we’ve promised that we would focus certainly on affordability and driving down the high cost of living, and on accountability in the face of the unprecedented corruption that we’ve seen unleashed on the American people by the Trump cartel," Jeffries said. "We’re committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it’s found. That’s in Congress, in the Supreme Court and with respect to this administration."
For its part, the administration is saying it will investigate Democrats. Trump said Saturday that he ordered the Department of Justice to examine what he deemed "criminal" acts by Democrats, though he did not provide examples to support his allegations. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday echoed the president's statement.
"What we've seen over the past several days and even over the past several weeks are outright threats, many, many by elected members of Congress and some senators against anybody that's conservative and anybody that that happens to be a Republican," Blanche told CNN. "Over the last several days, we've seen it, that rhetoric even rise up to the point where they're already -- before they're even in power, they're already talking about investigations and impeachments with no basis, no facts, just out there running around -- that that should be something that that President Trump is very concerned about. And certainly I am as well."
